answer_text:
Let

\[
S=a+b+c,\qquad L=[a,b]+[b,c]+[c,a].
\]

The expression is

\[
E=\frac S2-\frac LS.
\]

We will prove that

\[
E\ge \frac32,
\]

and then show equality is attainable.

Since \(S>0\),

\[
E-\frac32
= \frac S2-\frac LS-\frac32
= \frac{S(S-3)-2L}{2S}.
\]

Thus it is enough to prove

\[
2L\le S(S-3).
\]

Because \([x,y]\le xy\) for positive integers \(x,y\),

\[
L\le ab+bc+ca.
\]

Let \(Q=ab+bc+ca\). We compare \(Q\) with \(\frac{S(S-3)}2\):

\[
Q-\frac{S(S-3)}2
= \frac{2Q-S^2+3S}{2}.
\]

But

\[
S^2=a^2+b^2+c^2+2Q,
\]

so

\[
2Q-S^2+3S=3S-(a^2+b^2+c^2)
= -\bigl(a(a-3)+b(b-3)+c(c-3)\bigr).
\]

Therefore,

\[
Q\le \frac{S(S-3)}2
\iff
a(a-3)+b(b-3)+c(c-3)\ge 0.
\]

For an integer \(n>1\),

\[
n(n-3)=
\begin{cases}
-2, & n=2,\\
0, & n=3,\\
\ge 4, & n\ge 4.
\end{cases}
\]

If at least one of \(a,b,c\) is at least \(4\), then

\[
a(a-3)+b(b-3)+c(c-3)\ge 4-2-2=0.
\]

Hence in that case,

\[
2L\le 2Q\le S(S-3).
\]

If none of \(a,b,c\) is at least \(4\), then all are either \(2\) or \(3\). We check the four possibilities up to permutation:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
(a,b,c) & S & L & S(S-3)-2L\\
\hline
(2,2,2) & 6 & 6 & 6\\
(2,2,3) & 7 & 14 & 0\\
(2,3,3) & 8 & 15 & 10\\
(3,3,3) & 9 & 9 & 36
\end{array}
\]

Thus in all cases,

\[
2L\le S(S-3),
\]

so

\[
E\ge \frac32.
\]

Equality occurs for \((a,b,c)=(2,2,3)\) and its permutations. Indeed,

\[
S=7,\qquad L=[2,2]+[2,3]+[3,2]=2+6+6=14,
\]

and

\[
E=\frac72-\frac{14}{7}=\frac72-2=\frac32.
\]

Therefore, the minimum value is

\[
\boxed{\frac32}.
\]
